analysis.one_liner: Froze new endangered species listings and made taxpayers pay landowners for habitat-designation losses.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single vote, despite 20 Republican cosponsors, leaving Endangered Species Act protections untouched.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned the Interior Department from listing any new endangered or threatened species or designating any new critical habitat until the Endangered Species Act was reauthorized. It would also have required the government to pay private landowners any drop in their land's market value caused by a critical habitat designation, and it suspended the rules that keep federal agencies from harming endangered species. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Private landowners, real estate developers, and agriculture, timber, mining, and energy interests whose property or projects would otherwise face restrictions from new species listings or critical habitat designations. Landowners would gain an on-demand right to taxpayer compensation for any market-value loss, and developers and resource industries would face no new species-related land-use limits during the moratorium.

how_it_helps.text: Private landowners could demand payment from the Interior Department for any loss in market value of their land resulting from a critical habitat designation, converting a regulatory restriction into a government-paid claim.

The bill barred any new endangered or threatened species listings and any new critical habitat designations until the Act was reauthorized, so no property would face new species-related restrictions in the meantime.

Federal agencies would be exempt until reauthorization from the Endangered Species Act's core duties, including conserving listed species and ensuring their actions do not jeopardize a species' existence or destroy its habitat, easing approval of government-backed projects.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who would fund an open-ended obligation to compensate landowners for market-value losses with no stated funding source or cap, and the public, which would lose the Endangered Species Act's protection for at-risk species — some of which could decline or vanish before any reauthorization.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium on new listings and critical habitat designations means species discovered to be in trouble would receive no federal protection until reauthorization, which had no fixed date — leaving imperiled species with potentially nothing during the freeze.

The compensation mandate is an unlimited taxpayer liability: whenever a critical habitat designation lowers land value, the government must pay on request, with no appropriation, cap, or offset in the bill.
Suspending the requirement that federal actions not jeopardize endangered species or destroy their habitat removes the Act's central check on dams, logging, drilling, and other government projects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are targeted and concrete: property owners and resource interests gain either freedom from new restrictions or a taxpayer check. The costs are diffuse and large: an open-ended compensation bill for taxpayers, a freeze on protecting newly imperiled species of indefinite length, and suspension of the safeguards that keep federal projects from wiping out species. The bill transfers a public conservation program's costs and obligations toward private interests while suspending its purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or floor time before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lamar Smith of Texas introduced the Farm, Ranch, and Homestead Protection Act of 1995 on January 11, 1995, and it was referred to the House Committee on Resources the same day.
Twenty House Republicans signed on as cosponsors, all from Smith's own party.
On January 23, 1995, the House requested an executive comment from the Interior Department, but no markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed.
The bill sat in committee until the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, so the Endangered Species Act's listing, habitat, and federal-agency protections all remained in force.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Endangered species and the public's existing protections came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, no new-listing moratorium, landowner compensation mandate, or exemption for federal agencies ever took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Species protections and the general public

for.name: Rep. Lamar Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and drove it through referral

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or reported the bill, letting it die when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred to test support, but all 20 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican.

industries.industry: Real estate development and private landholders
industries.note: Developers and large landowners would gain a right to taxpayer compensation whenever a critical habitat designation lowered their land's value, and no new land would be restricted during the listing moratorium. Their gain comes directly out of the public's conservation protections and the treasury.

The bill's namesake constituency would escape new habitat restrictions on ranch and farm land and could claim compensation for existing designations. The cost shifts to taxpayers and to species on working lands.

industries.industry: Timber, mining, and oil and gas
industries.note: Resource extraction on both private and federal land would face no new species constraints, since agencies would be freed from the duty to avoid jeopardizing species or destroying habitat.

Businesses and communities that depend on healthy fish and wildlife — guides, outfitters, recreational fishing and tourism — would lose the federal backstop that keeps at-risk species from sliding toward extinction.
